scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pachanga originated in Cuba in 1959, created by Eduardo Davidson.
It migrated to New York City during the post-WWII wave of Cuban immigration, finding a home in Bronx venues like the Caravana Club and the Triton After-Hours Club.
on_screen: Map: Cuba · Caribbean

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically a social dance craze in 1950s/60s ballrooms, it is now a performance element in salsa shines.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed on the downbeat of 4/4 time.
It is highly grounded, requiring the dancer to maintain a constant bend in the knees.
The core movement is a double-bend and straighten of the knees, which facilitates a gliding weight transfer.
Watch for Bronx Hop.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (BwjN0t7eFPU)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Solo shines or partnerwork.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Pachanga is played by charanga ensembles, which utilize violins, flutes, drums, piano, and bass.
The music is a blend of son montuno, merengue, and conga.
Listen for the violin, flute, drums, piano.
The pulse is 4/4.
A lively, syncopated sound driven by the interplay between high-pitched violins and flutes, supported by a rhythmic foundation of drums and piano.
